rows.stem: A boy developed some allergic reactions when he straight entered into his air conditioned room after a game of football outside his house. Write any two symptoms that could be noticed in such condition. How does our body combat such conditions ?

(i) Write the Scientific name of the plant from where natural cannabinoids are obtained.
(ii) Mention the parts of the plant that are used for extracting the drug.
(iii) How does the drug affect human body ?
rows.solution:
(i) Natural cannabinoids are obtained from the inflorescences of the plant **Cannabis sativa**.

(ii) Any two of: the **flower tops (inflorescences)**, the **leaves** and the **resin** of the plant. Their combinations are used to make marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja.

(iii) Cannabinoids are generally taken by inhalation and oral ingestion, and they are known for their effects on the **cardiovascular system** of the body.

rows.stem: Epithelial lining of our intestine is considered as secondary lymphoid organ. Justify the statement.
rows.solution:
The epithelial lining of the intestine carries the **mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)**, located within the lining of the major tracts (respiratory, digestive and urogenital). It constitutes about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue in the human body.

It counts as a secondary lymphoid organ because, like the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils and Peyer's patches:
- it **provides the site for interaction of lymphocytes with the antigen**;
- there the lymphocytes **proliferate to become effector cells**.

(Primary lymphoid organs, the bone marrow and thymus, are where lymphocytes are produced and mature; secondary lymphoid organs are where the matured lymphocytes meet antigens.)

rows.stem:
Farmers are often suggested to use the following organisms in their crop land so as to improve the soil fertility.
(i) Rhizobium (ii) Anabaena
Explain.
rows.solution:
Both are **biofertilisers**, organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil.

(i) **Rhizobium** forms a **symbiotic association with the roots of leguminous plants**, living in their root nodules, where it **fixes atmospheric nitrogen** into organic forms usable by the plant.

(ii) **Anabaena** is a cyanobacterium (an autotrophic microbe) that **fixes atmospheric nitrogen in aquatic and terrestrial environments**, for example in paddy fields. It serves as an important biofertiliser and also **adds organic matter to the soil**, increasing its fertility.

rows.stem: Organic farmer use Trichoderma and Baculovirus as biological control agents. Explain.
Mammals are capable of maintaining homeostasis. But, very few smaller animals can survive in polar regions. Give reasons.
rows.solution:
Mammals keep a constant body temperature, but doing so costs energy, and the cost is highest for small animals:
- **Heat loss or heat gain is a function of surface area.** Small animals have a **large surface area relative to their volume**.
- So they **lose body heat very fast** when it is cold outside, as in the polar regions during severe winters.
- They then have to **expend much energy to generate body heat through metabolism**, which they cannot sustain for long.

This is why very few small animals are found in polar regions, and those that live in cold places avoid the stress in time, by **hibernation** during winter or by **migration** to warmer areas.

rows.stem:
Observe the schematic representation given above and answer the following questions :
(i) Identify A and B.
(ii) Calculate the growth rate of bacteria in a curd sample, where 1 million bacteria increased to two million, within a period of one hour.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a schematic of a box labelled Population D, with an arrow labelled Immigration at the top and an arrow labelled Emigration at the bottom, and two circled labels joined to the box by arrows, B on the left and A on the right. Which of A and B points into the box and which points out of it decides the answer to (i), so the arrow directions are withheld here. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
(i)
- **A: mortality**, the number of deaths in the population, which removes individuals from it.
- **B: natality**, the number of births in the population, which adds individuals to it.

Together with immigration (which adds) and emigration (which removes), these are the four basic processes that change the density of a population.

(ii) The growth rate here is the increase in number per individual per unit time:

\(\text{Growth rate} = \dfrac{2 \text{ million} - 1 \text{ million}}{1 \text{ million}} = 1\)

So the growth rate is **1 bacterium per bacterium per hour**.

rows.stem: Identify the type of pyramid given above. Write the identifying feature on the basis of which you identified it.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a stepped pyramid of horizontal bars split by a vertical centre line, in three shaded bands labelled (top to bottom) Post Reproductive, Reproductive and Pre Reproductive. The relative widths of the bands decide the type of pyramid, so they are withheld here. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
- It is an **age pyramid** of the **expanding** (increasing, growing) type.
- Identifying feature: the number of individuals in the **pre-reproductive** age group is **more than** that in the **reproductive** age group, which in turn is more than the post-reproductive group, so the pyramid has a broad base.

A broad pre-reproductive base means many young individuals will soon enter the reproductive age, so the population is growing. (A stable population gives a bell-shaped pyramid, and a declining one an urn-shaped pyramid with a narrow base.)

rows.stem:
(a) Write the complete name of the diagnostic test for AIDS. Explain the principle it works on.
(b) Name the type of genetic material present in AIDS causing pathogen.
rows.solution:
(a) The widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is **ELISA**, the **Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay**. It works on the principle of **antigen-antibody interaction**: HIV infection is detected either by the presence of the virus's **antigens** (proteins, glycoproteins) or by detecting the **antibodies synthesised against the pathogen** in the patient's blood.

The marking scheme also accepts **PCR (polymerase chain reaction)**, which allows **early detection** of HIV by **amplifying the genetic material of the virus**, even when its concentration is very low.

(b) The AIDS-causing pathogen, the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), is a **retrovirus**, so its genetic material is **RNA**.

rows.stem:
A patient complains of suffering from constipation, stomach ache, stool with blood clots and excess mucous. The physician diagnosed it as amoebiasis, after stool test.
(a) Write the scientific name of the microbe identified in the stool sample.
(b) How do you think, the patient must have contracted it ?
(c) Write your suggestions to the patient to avoid infection in future.
What are cry-proteins ? With the help of a suitable example, explain how it acts as a biological pesticide.
rows.solution:
- **Cry proteins** are the **toxic insecticidal proteins** (crystal proteins) produced by the bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis** (Bt). They are coded by the genes named **cry**.
- Example: in **Bt cotton**, the genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworms; in **Bt corn**, cryIAb protects against the corn borer. (Bt varieties of rice, tomato and soyabean are other examples.)
- How it acts as a biological pesticide:
  - The Bt toxin exists as an **inactive protoxin**, so it does not harm the bacterium or the transgenic plant.
  - Once an insect eats it, the inactive toxin is **converted into the active form by the alkaline pH of the insect's gut**, which solubilises the crystals.
  - The activated toxin **binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells** and **creates pores**, causing **swelling and lysis** of the cells and eventually **the death of the insect**.

rows.stem: Explain the concept of "co-extinction" by taking two examples.
rows.solution:
**Co-extinction**: when a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an **obligatory way** also become extinct.

Examples (any two):
- When a **host fish species becomes extinct**, its unique assemblage of **parasites** also meets the same fate, since they cannot live without that host.
- In a **coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism**, the extinction of one partner leads to the extinction of the other. For example, the Mediterranean orchid **Ophrys** depends on one particular species of **bee** for pollination; if the bee were lost, the orchid would also be lost, and vice versa.

rows.stem: "Forests provide intangible benefits to us." Explain by taking three different areas, how.
rows.solution:
Besides their direct economic products, forests give us benefits that cannot be priced or traded, the broadly utilitarian and ethical reasons for conserving them. Three areas:
- **Ecological services:** forests (the Amazon forest alone is estimated to produce about 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere) are a major **source of oxygen** through photosynthesis.
- **Pollination:** forests support bees, bumblebees, birds and bats, the pollinators **without which plants cannot produce fruits or seeds**.
- **Aesthetic pleasure:** walking through thick woods, watching spring flowers in full bloom, or waking up to a bulbul's song in the morning give us joy that cannot be measured.

The marking scheme also accepts other benefits, such as contribution to **traditional medicines** used by native people, and the **ethical (spiritual) value**: every species has an intrinsic value, even if it is of no current economic value to us, and we have a moral duty to care for the millions of plants, animals and microbes with which we share this planet.

rows.stem:
(a) Given below is the stepwise schematic representation of the process of electrophoresis. Identify the 'alphabets' representing (i) Anode end (ii) smallest/lightest DNA strand in the matrix (iii) Agarose gel
(b) What is elution ? State the importance of elution in this process.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a rectangle drawn as a gel with four lanes numbered 1 to 4 (bottom to top), each starting from an open rectangular well at the left and carrying a row of vertical band marks; circled labels P, Q and R point down into lane 4 from above, a circled label T points up into lane 1 from below, and the left and right edges are marked 'end' with circled labels U (left) and S (right). Which feature each letter marks, and so which end is the anode, decides part (a) and is withheld here. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
(a) In gel electrophoresis the DNA fragments are loaded in the wells at one end and, being **negatively charged**, move through the **agarose gel matrix** towards the **anode** (positive electrode) at the other end. The fragments separate by size, because the matrix has a sieving effect: the **smaller the fragment, the farther it moves**.
- (i) Anode end: **S**, the end towards which the bands have moved, away from the wells.
- (ii) Smallest/lightest DNA strand: **R**, the band that has moved farthest from its well.
- (iii) Agarose gel: **T**.

(b) **Elution** is the process of **cutting out the separated bands of DNA from the agarose gel and extracting the DNA** from the gel piece. The separated DNA is first made visible by staining with ethidium bromide and exposing it to UV light, where it shows as bright orange bands.

Importance: elution gives **purified DNA fragments**, which are then used in constructing **recombinant DNA** by joining them with cloning vectors, and in other genetic experiments.

rows.subtopic: Isolation, Cutting and Amplification of DNA
rows.stem: Taq polymerase after its discovery replaced E.coli DNA polymerase in PCR technique. Explain giving reasons why was the need felt for the change ?
rows.context: Enzyme Taq polymerase, is extracted from a eubacterial microorganism Thermus aquaticus from Yellowstone National Park in Montana, USA and isolated by Chien et al. (1976). Taq polymerase successfully replaced the DNA polymerase from E.coli that was being used in PCR earlier and this shift revolutionised the PCR technique.
rows.solution:
- In PCR the DNA is repeatedly **heated to a high temperature** to denature it, that is, to separate its two strands. The **E.coli DNA polymerase cannot carry out PCR at such high temperatures**, because it becomes **inactive (denatured)**, so fresh enzyme would have to be added after every cycle.
- **Taq polymerase**, isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, is **thermostable**: it **remains active even at the high temperatures** used to denature the DNA. So the reaction can run through many cycles without adding fresh enzyme, which made PCR fast and automatable.

rows.subtopic: Isolation, Cutting and Amplification of DNA
rows.stem: What is a primer and its importance in PCR ?
rows.context: Enzyme Taq polymerase, is extracted from a eubacterial microorganism Thermus aquaticus from Yellowstone National Park in Montana, USA and isolated by Chien et al. (1976). Taq polymerase successfully replaced the DNA polymerase from E.coli that was being used in PCR earlier and this shift revolutionised the PCR technique.
rows.solution:
- **Primers** are **small, chemically synthesised oligonucleotides** that are **complementary to the regions of the DNA** (the ends of the region to be amplified on the genomic DNA strands).
- Importance: in PCR two sets of primers anneal to the separated strands, and the **DNA polymerase extends them**, using the nucleotides provided, to **synthesise the complementary DNA strand**. A DNA polymerase cannot start a new strand on its own, so without primers there would be no extension and no amplification.

rows.stem: Write the importance of PCR as a diagnostic tool.
rows.context: Enzyme Taq polymerase, is extracted from a eubacterial microorganism Thermus aquaticus from Yellowstone National Park in Montana, USA and isolated by Chien et al. (1976). Taq polymerase successfully replaced the DNA polymerase from E.coli that was being used in PCR earlier and this shift revolutionised the PCR technique.
rows.solution: PCR allows **early detection of diseases** such as cancer, AIDS (HIV) or a genetic disorder by **amplifying the nucleic acid** of the pathogen or of the desired (mutated) gene. It can detect a pathogen even when its **concentration is very low**, before the symptoms of the disease appear, which is much earlier than conventional methods (serum and urine analysis) allow.

rows.stem:
(i) Name the human disease for which the gene therapy was used for the first time.
(ii) Explain the steps of gene therapy carried to cure the disease using the lymphocytes of the patient. Why is this therapy not a permanent cure of the disease ?
(iii) Write the possible permanent cure of the disease by the gene therapy that is in progress.
rows.context: Biotechnology revolves around the "gene of interest", with an objective to open various avenues for human welfare in health, medicine, pharma, agriculture etc. using different techniques, tools and processes. One of the breakthroughs of biotechnology in medicine is the gene therapy.
rows.solution:
(i) The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with **adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency**. The enzyme ADA is crucial for the immune system to function, and its deficiency is caused by the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase.

(ii) Steps of the gene therapy:
- **Lymphocytes** from the blood of the patient are **grown in a culture outside the body**.
- A **functional ADA cDNA** is then introduced into these lymphocytes **using a retroviral vector**.
- The genetically modified lymphocytes are subsequently **returned (injected) to the patient's body**.

It is not a permanent cure because **these lymphocytes are not immortal**: they die after some time, so the patient **requires periodic infusion** of such genetically engineered lymphocytes.

(iii) A possible permanent cure: the **gene isolated from bone marrow cells producing ADA** is introduced into cells at an **early embryonic stage**. Since these cells keep dividing and giving rise to the immune cells, the corrected gene would be carried permanently.
